content_metadata.description: An educational video explaining the SAMR model using playdough and a tennis ball.

qAndA.answer: The first level is Substitution, where new technology replaces old technology but does not change the task.
qAndA.question: What is the first level of the SAMR model?

qAndA.answer: The video mentions the ability to share a Google Doc in one click and the fact that it automatically saves to the cloud as examples of Augmentation because they increase the functionality of a word processor.
qAndA.question: What is an example of Augmentation in the SAMR model?

qAndA.answer: The video uses a blue ball of playdough to represent the Modification level.
qAndA.question: What visual representation is used for the Modification level in the video?

qAndA.answer: The video suggests that connecting to a classroom across the world through Google Docs, allowing students to write narratives of the same historical event and discuss the differences using chat and comment features, is an example of Redefinition.
qAndA.question: What example of Redefinition is given in the video?

qAndA.answer: The choice of a tennis ball for Redefinition is likely intended to symbolize a significant shift or transformation, highlighting the move away from merely replacing or enhancing tasks to creating entirely new possibilities. The tennis ball stands out from the playdough blocks, visually suggesting a departure from the traditional and a leap into new territory.
qAndA.question: Why is the tennis ball chosen to represent Redefinition?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: This is the same model in 120 seconds.
The same model is a framework that provides a lens for viewing technology integration
in the classroom.
The first level is substitution or the idea that a block is a block no matter where it is
or how you access it.
This would be like using Google Docs as any other word processor.
The new tech replaces the old tech but it does not change the task.
The next level is augmentation.
At this level, the tech is still a substitute but provides more functionality as students
work to complete the same task.
The ability to share your Google Doc in one click and the fact that it saves to the cloud
automatically and provides you access from anywhere is an increase in functionality.
The next level is modification.
Here the ball really gets rolling because the technology is used to redesign parts of
the task and transform student learning.
This is collaborating on one Google Doc and using the comment feature to provide instant
feedback as an example of modification.
The final level of Samar is redefinition.
At this level we're able to design and create new tasks that were once unimaginable.
By shifting our perspective from technology just being another block or substitute, we're
able to truly start imagining the possibilities.
An example of redefinition would be connecting to a classroom across the world through student
sharing Google Docs.
They would each write their own narrative of the same historical event using the chat
and comment section to discuss the differences.
Then students would use the voice comments app to discuss the differences they noticed
and embed this in their class website as a culture walk.
To recap, substitution is the same task new tech replaces old tech.
Augmentation is the same task but the tech increases functionality.
Modification were able to redesign parts of the task.
Redefination were able to create new tasks once unimaginable.
As we move from substitution to redefinition we're moving from enhancing to transforming
student learning.

youtube_description: This is a quick introduction to the SAMR Model, developed by Dr. Ruben Puentedura. It is not meant to be an in-depth view of the model.  For more information, visit http://hippasus.com/.
